pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written rnn.t or rnnwtt; conventionally vocalised “Renenutet”. The root rnn means “to nurse, suckle”.
The cobra-goddess of the harvest and of nursing, lady of the granary.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Τηρνοῦθις (Tērnoûthis); fused with Thermouthis in the Greco-Roman period

pronunciation.note: Her name is the participle “she who nurses” — the harvest that feeds is her milk.

domains.title: Goddess of the Harvest, the Nursing Cobra
domains.subtitle: Lady of the Granary, Mother of the Field
domains.lead: Rnnwtt — Renenutet — is the harvest as maternity: the cobra who coils in the last standing sheaf and nurses the grain to ripeness. Every Egyptian granary was her temple in miniature; every nurse suckling a child repeated her oldest work. She is the goddess in whom food and motherhood are the same fact.

cards.name: The Harvest Cobra
cards.desc: A rearing cobra crowned with the harvest’s plumes; the last sheaf of the field is her shrine.

cards.name: Lady of the Granary
cards.desc: Every storehouse and threshing floor fell under her protection — and her audit.

cards.name: The Nursing Goddess
cards.desc: Her name means “she who nurses”; the pharaoh himself was her nursling.

cards.name: Goddess of the Vineyard
cards.desc: Wine-presses and wine-jars carried her name; the vintage was her second harvest.

mythology.lead: Renenutet’s mythology is the theology of food security in a subsistence economy: the goddess who turns sunlight into grain and grain into children’s milk. She has no great narrative cycle because she needed none — every harvest was her epiphany, every famine her absence, every granary her chapel.

myths.title: The Cobra in the Last Sheaf
myths.text: Egyptian reapers left the last sheaf standing and addressed it as Renenutet: the goddess still resident in the field. To cut it was to release her into the granary for the year’s safekeeping. The custom — attested from the Old Kingdom harvest scenes onward — made every field’s end a small theological drama.

myths.title: Mother of the Vineyard
myths.text: In the Fayum and at Dendera she presided over the wine-press as over the threshing-floor; the wine-jar docket ‘Renenutet’s portion’ marked the divine tithe of the vintage. With Sobek as her consort in the Fayum she mothered the crop-cycle whole — grain, grape, and the flood that feeds both.

myths.title: Nurse of the King
myths.text: The king’s titulary calls him ‘the nursling of Renenutet’: the harvest feeds the state as the breast feeds the child, and both are her body. Royal birth-scenes show her cobra rearing behind the throne of the nursing mother, transferring the goddess’ own milk into the legitimate succession.

myths.title: Thermouthis
myths.text: Under the Ptolemies she was worshipped as Thermouthis — ‘the harvest-serpent’ in Greek dress — with a cult that joined her to Isis the nurse. The equation made her an international goddess of provisioning, and her images spread with the grain trade she embodied.

lore.syncretism: Renenutet merged early with Wadjet, the cobra of Lower Egypt — both are the rearing uraeus — and with Meretseger of the Theban necropolis in her serpent aspect. As Thermouthis she was equated with Isis and Demeter, the two great maternal goddesses of the classical world; the triangulation made her the most exported of Egypt’s agricultural deities.
lore.culturalLegacy: The ‘last sheaf’ custom survived in Egyptian folk practice into the modern era, one of the longest-lived ritual continuities on earth. Her name, in the Greek dress of Thermouthis, entered the magical papyri and the romance-literature of the ancient novel; and every study of Egyptian food-economy begins with her shrines at the granary door.
lore.extendedMeditation: Rnnwtt: the name suckles. Its restoration in plain letters is a granary-stela — six consonants standing like six full jars in a row, each one sealed, each one feeding the next. No diacritic could improve a name that means milk.

sources.name: Harvest and vintage scenes, Old Kingdom tombs
Dendera granary dockets and wine tithes

lore.archaeology: Her finest surviving monument is the temple of Dendera’s granary quarter; the Fayum’s Tebtunis papyri preserve her vineyard accounts. Serpent-cult objects from the harvest festivals — plumed cobra figurines — fill the Late Period strata of sites across the valley.
lore.cult: Every threshing-floor kept her image; the harvest’s end brought her festival of the last sheaf. Nurses and mothers wore her amulets, and the state’s grain-auditors sealed their measures in her name — she was simultaneously pantry-goddess and auditor of the realm’s food.
lore.iconography: A rearing cobra, hood flared, crowned with two plumes or horns and sun-disc; in anthropomorphic form a woman with the cobra-head nursing a child. The sheaf, the wine-jar and the plough accompany her in harvest scenes.
lore.reception: Through Thermouthis she entered the Isis-circles of the Roman Empire, and her ‘last sheaf’ rite was recorded by every traveller who saw the Egyptian harvest from Herodotus to the nineteenth century. Modern agricultural anthropology still cites her as the type-case of the harvest-mother goddess.
